analytic.title: Probabilistic Worst Case Response Time Estimation for Multi-Core Real-Time Systems

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Traditional methods rely on Static Timing Analysis techniques to compute the Worst Case Response Time for tasks in real-time systems. Multi-Core real-time systems are faced up with concurrent task executions, semaphore accesses, and task migrations where it may be difficult to obtain the worst case upper bound. A new three staged probabilistic estimation concept is presented. Worst Case Response Times are estimated for tasksets which consist of tasks with multiple time bases. The concept involves data generation with sample classification and sample size equalization, model fit and Worst Case Response Time estimation on the basis of extreme value distribution models. A Generalized Pareto Distribution model fit method which includes threshold detection and parameter estimation is also presented. Sample classification in combination with the new Generalized Pareto Distribution model fit method allows to estimate Worst Case Response Times with low pessimism ranges compared to estimation methods that uses the Generalized Pareto or the Gumbel max distribution without sample classification.

div.head: INTRODUCTION
div.p: The number of embedded automotive systems significantly increases per year. More than 100 electronic control units (ECUs) are build in today's cars, where they fulfill important functions (for example the control of the combustion engine). Traditional approaches use deterministic analysis to approximate bounds on task response times. Static Timing Analysis (STA) is a common method in literature to calculate the Worst Case Response Time (WCRT) for tasks. Today, multi-core processor systems are state-of-the-art automotive power-train systems. The traditional STA requires knowledge about the upper response time bound of the task. In multi-core real-time systems, it may be difficult to obtain these upper time bound. Therefore new methods are required, that consider these delays and interruptions to estimate the WCRT. Edgar and Burns [1] where the first in 2001, who introduced a probabilistic timing analysis approach. They estimated the WCET of tasks by using the Gumbel max extreme value distribution. In 2010, Griffin and Burns [2] compute WCET estimates with independent and identically distributed (iid) samples. Liu et al. [3] applied in 2013 the Generalized Pareto Distribution (GPD) on iid samples to estimate the WCRT for tasks in complex real-time systems.

div.head: II. CONTRIBUTION AND OUTLINE
div.p: This work continues the probabilistic timing analysis approach for multi-core real-time systems where a taskset in a typical automotive power-train system consists of tasks with Multiple Time Bases (MTB). A classification for unimodal / multimodal sample distributions is presented in Section V and the new job property execution-delay is introduced. A new WCRT estimation flow is introduced for tasksets that are simulated t time units. A new GPD model fit concept is used to detect the threshold and estimate the model parameters. The contribution is structured as follows: Section III describes the application model and notation. Section IV gives a short introduction about the simulation approach and Section V shows the classification for sample distributions. Section VI introduces the three staged probabilistic WCRT estimation concept which is validated in Section VII. Section VIII concludes the contribution and propose future work.

div.head: III. APPLICATION MODEL AND NOTATION
div.p: This contribution assumes a Symmetric Multiprocessor (SMP) system as underlying hardware architecture.It consists of m identical processors which share one physical address et of m tasks T i . Each task T i owns timing properties and applies one of three activation patterns: periodic (time-triggered), engine-triggered, or sporadic. These patterns are comprised as MTB model; it refers to the work in [4]. A task instance is defined as the j th job J i,j of task T i . Fig. 1 shows general timing metrics of a job. Job J i,j can exclusively access a resource via a semaphore in the shared address space, i.e. to write data. D(j) denotes the job deadline and R(j) the job recurrence. The processing unit model defines different processing units, having individual processing speeds. Both, a topology as well as a behavior model description are included in the memory model. The topology defines the different memory modules, the caches, read/write buffer as well the networks which interconnect these modules and which processing unit can access which memory module via which path. On the other side, the behavior model defines properties like bus-arbitration priorities, caching policies for load and write-back behavior. The scheduling of the application is described in the operating system model. Here, global or local scheduler can be selected with different scheduling algorithms, managing the assignment of task instances to processing units of the hardware model. The case studies in section VII apply OSEK scheduling. It belongs to the class of local scheduler. The access of global read /write variables is managed with global scheduler and not part of this work. The software model describes the workload of the application. For each task a call graph is defined, including basic blocks which can have a simple amount of processor cycles or additionally blocking or non-blocking accesses to hardware elements, e.g. memory modules, semaphores, etc. The activation of a task and the amount of processor cycles can be described by probability functions, having at least a minimum and a maximum value. During simulation, sampling mechanisms generate sequences of processor cycle demands for a basic block, according to the probabilistic function.

div.head: V. CLASSIFICATION OF SAMPLE DISTRIBUTIONS
div.p: Worst case response time estimation approaches use extremal distributions as underlying models. Extremal distributions are long or short tailed. WCRT estimations of tasks T i assume samples S i,t = {X 1 ,…,X n } with iid random variables because of model simplification. Random variables used in the WCRT estimation concept are response times rt j or normalized response times NRT j . Let S z = {X 1 ,…,X n } denote a sample of random variables with size n. S z is iid correct if each X in S z is independent to any other random variable and all X in S z come from the same distribution. Ideal samples for WCRT estimations are univariate right-skewed with a long tail, where random variables over a high threshold can be observed. The Pareto distribution family fits these samples best. Univariate sample values come from one metric and are not influenced by another one. Right-skewed samples without random variables over a high threshold are modeled with distributions of the Generalized Extreme Value distribution (GEV) family. The WCRT estimation approach in Section VI applies Pareto I and GPD from the Pareto distribution family, and Gumbel max from the GEV family. The assumption of ideal samples holds for tasks T i with non-execution-delayed jobs J i,j . Job related execution-delays

They are attributed to missing data, caused by task interruptions.

div.head: VI. THREE STAGED PROBABILISTIC WCRT ESTIMATION CONCEPT
div.p: The following subsections present the three staged probabilistic WCRT estimation concept (Fig. 2

div.head: A. Data Generation
div.p: The estimation quality of statistical approaches depends T i may own different periods and activation pattern. This involves a different amount of activated jobs J i,j per task T i and leads to different response time sample sizes n per task. Thus, we introduce in the following a technique (Fig. 2 This approach is a generalized form of task sample size equalization and can be applied on any taskset. Sample data in this contribution comes from tasks with periodic, enginetriggered, or sporadic activation. Jobs from sporadic tasks occur randomly within the scheduled time. Their response times are independent and identically distributed. This assertion is false for periodic and engine-triggered tasks. Each job J i,j of task T i depends on its previous job J i,j-1 and likewise their appropriate response times. The data generation stage uses a Block Maxima (BM) sampling variant to fulfill iid correctness. Here, a task sample S i,t that comes from one simulation is equivalent to a block. The maximal response time from each task sample S i,t is determined in every simulation and a sample of maxima S m,r is constructed for each task, so that S m,r = {max(S i,1 ),…,max(S i,nt )}. This sampling method collects maximal response times from the right upper bound of each S i,t with same sample size np. The simulation is initialized in every run to avoid dependencies between collected maxima in S m;r . The Turning-Point hypothesis test [7] [8] with significance level = 5% is applied on each S m,r to test iid correctness. Stage II in the following subsection VI-B uses the sample of maxima S m,r to determine its distribution.

div.head: B. Sample Classification & Model Fit
div.p: This stage uses Goodness-Of-Fit (GoF) tests to assign one of the distributions that are specified in table II for each S m,r . Given that S m,r is unimodal distributed, an extreme value model can be fit on it and the WCRT can be estimated. The WCRT is computed in multimodal distributions without model fit in stage III. Unimodality is tested with Hartigan's dip test [9]. If the dip test passes, two Kolmogorov-Smirnov (KS) GoF tests check whether S m,r comes from a GPD or Gumbel max distribution. The KS GoF test computes the maximum distance between the empirical (sample distribution) and the fit (model distribution) CDF. Unknown parameters to fit the model on the sample are estimated with the Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) method. Maximum likelihood estimates are those parameters that maximize the sample likelihood. Both KS GoF tests are parametrized with significance level = 5%. With the GPD as tail distribution, WCRTs are estimated more in detail compared to the Gumbel max distribution. Precondition to fit the GPD model is the computed threshold μ. It marks the beginning of the tail distribution in S m,r . This approach uses an iterative threshold detection method with the distance metric .

div.head: C. WCRT Estimation
div.p: WCRT estimation depends on the fitted distribution model in stage II. There exists a percent point function for the GPD and Gumbel max to estimate the WCRT for a given probability p. The WCRT is underestimated, if n p is small. Sample size n p is obtained on the basis of the Margin of Error as described in subsection VI-A. This contribution uses a ME of 3% where n p = 1067.

div.head: VII. CASE STUDY
div.p: The case study compares the WCRT estimation for different system confidence levels and test correct sampletodistribution model classification. Sample of maxima S m,r consist of response times rt j , which are normalized by their task deadlines D i . With deadline normalized response time samples (NRT j ), estimated WCRTs can be compared against each other and deadline misses can be detected. Table III depicts the taskset for the case study. Taskset simulation is performed using the TA-Simulator on a CUDA PC equipped with an Intel i7 3.2 GHz processor, 16 GB RAM, and Windows 7. The hardware model of the TA-Simulator consists of a dual core processor with 40 MHz and an OSEK scheduler for each core. OSEK is the standard scheduler for power-train systems. The normalized WCRT for multimodal distributions is marked with the label "Simulation" in Fig. 4. Fig. 4 depicts a significant pessimism increase for Gumbel max WCRT estimates. Task T1MS has the highest increase of pessimism and the highest pessimism range from 24% to 61% compared to all other tasks in Example II. System confidences above 1•10 -5 in Example II causes deadline misses. Moreover, tasks with semaphore access pass the GPD KS test with the presented task set configuration.

WCRTs are estimated in stage III with the GPD or Gumbel max point process, if S m,r is unimodal distributed. GPD threshold detection and parameter estimation is done with the new iterative threshold detection method. It detects GPD parameters that fits the S m,r for a minimal error . This method allows to estimate WCRTs with low pessimism ranges for classified samples compared to estimation methods that are based on one distribution without sample classification. The WCRT in a multimodal distributed sample S m,r is the maximal response time in S m,r . In future work the authors want to find a solution to estimate multimodal distributed samples for different system confidences. Moreover, the presented WCRT estimation concept shall be parallelized. The workflow will then be able to estimate WCRTs in large-scaled tasksets for practical multicore real-time systems and to perform long-term studies.
